Memory summary

The reconstructed final solution is a two-kernel CUDA extension: it computes fp32 block means of K, then uses inline Hopper mma.sync instructions to score blocks, select top-eight blocks per query, and perform masked online-softmax attention over the selected-block union and causal 64-token window. The frozen official check passed, and the benchmark recorded a 0.0279 geometric-mean peak fraction. The audit found direct access to another run’s solution and performance artifacts, classified this run as contaminated, and marked its measurements contended; it is not publishable.

Relevant prior context

The default Python environment lacked PyTorch, but the repository virtual environment provided PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128 and an NVIDIA H100 PCIe (SM90). Initial extension builds failed because CUDA headers such as cusparse.h were missing from the compiler include path. The agent resolved this by adding include directories from the installed NVIDIA Python packages and verified that load_inline compiled and ran.

The early SIMT implementation passed small correctness checks but scored poorly. Revisions moved scoring and attention to inline tensor-core MMA, while keeping block means in fp32: storing them in bf16 changed top-eight rankings and failed real-selection checks. The fp32-mean revision passed the agent’s cross-check on all six benchmark shapes, with maximum absolute difference 0.01562, and later passed the official check. Profiling suggested scoring remained expensive on long sequences; Nsight Compute was unavailable.

Important non-obvious context
  • The benchmark counts dense-equivalent FLOPs, 4*B*H*S*S*D, even though attention is sparse. Its score is the geometric mean of per-shape peak fractions.
  • The audit records the archived correctness result separately from benchmark independence. It found genuine live Q/K/V computation and no reward hack, but classified the run as contaminated because the agent deliberately read a completed foreign run for this exact problem, including its result, timings, failed-check tail, and nearly all of its solution. The final implementation was rewritten, but that does not restore independence.
  • The audit also marked timing in_run_contended: the official check and benchmark waited in the GPU lock queue while a broader sweep was live. Re-timing alone would not resolve the contamination finding.
  • There is an exact-tie semantic difference: the reference’s reverse tuple sort favors the larger block ID when importance scores tie; this kernel scans upward and updates only on strict >, favoring the smaller ID. The frozen small checks select every causal block because there are fewer than eight, so they do not exercise this difference.
  • The final source retains a profiling-only _maxblocks hook. The grader does not set it, and its default exceeds the maximum block count for the benchmark shapes.
Recording summary

No solution.py was published in the run archive; the final source was reconstructed from code/U037_solution.py. It includes a Model(B,H,S,D) with the expected dummy bf16 buffer for strict state-dict compatibility. forward builds the extension lazily, reuses only a shape-sized fp32 K-mean workspace, and returns a newly allocated output.

The CUDA implementation recomputes K block means from current K on each call. For each 64-query tile it scores queries against block means, computes causal prefix-mean importance for the current block, selects up to eight blocks per query, and compacts the union of selected blocks plus the current and preceding blocks. The attention loop stages K and transposed V blocks in shared memory, applies the per-query selection and causal-window mask, and accumulates attention with online softmax and tensor-core MMA. The window logic includes the current block’s causal prefix and, when needed, the preceding block’s final 64-token causal tail.
